aws.label: Most reliable
aws.rationale: Survives an availability-zone failure: extra capacity and a standby database.

caveats: Assumes a commitment you have not made. The on-demand price is what you pay today.

caveats: Assumes a commitment you have not made. The on-demand price is what you pay today.

applied.name: ARM instances for the managed database
applied.summary: Run the managed PostgreSQL on ARM (db.t4g / db.m7g) instead of x86. Same engine, same behaviour, lower hourly rate — and unlike application compute there is nothing to rebuild, because the provider runs the database.
tradeoffs: Not every engine version is offered on ARM classes in every region
Migrating an existing instance class requires a maintenance window
Smaller selection of instance sizes than x86 in some regions

applied.name: Burstable instances for workloads that idle
applied.summary: T-family instances cost less per hour than fixed-performance families of the same size, and bank CPU credits while idle. For a workload that is mostly idle with occasional peaks, that is the correct shape.
tradeoffs: Sustained load exhausts credits. The failure is either throttling or a surcharge, and both are worse than having paid for the right shape.
Credit balance is another thing to monitor.
Not suitable for latency-sensitive work where a throttle is visible to a user.

applied.name: Commit to a year of usage (Savings Plan / Reserved / CUD)
applied.summary: Commit to a baseline level of compute for one year in exchange for a lower hourly rate. The largest single discount available on a steady workload, and the first thing any cost review applies.
applied.tool: AWS Cost Explorer — Savings Plans recommendations
tradeoffs: Locks in twelve months of spend whether or not the workload survives
Commit to the steady floor, not the peak — over-committing wastes more than it saves, and the unused commitment is still billed
Savings Plans keep instance-family freedom; Standard RIs are cheaper still but pin you to a family
Does not apply to spot capacity, which is already discounted further
reasons: steady baseline that will still be running in a year, so a one-year commitment is safe to take

applied.name: ARM-based compute (AWS Graviton / Azure Ampere / GCP Axion)
applied.summary: Run the same workload on ARM processors instead of x86. Comparable performance for most workloads, lower hourly price.
tradeoffs: Container images must be built for arm64 (multi-arch build required)
Rare x86-only dependencies (some proprietary agents, older native libs) will not run
Smaller instance-type selection than x86 in some regions
Real benefit may exceed the list-price gap if the workload performs better per core, but that requires benchmarking the specific workload

applied.name: Move cold objects to an infrequent-access class
applied.summary: Most of what a bucket holds is never read again after its first few weeks. A lifecycle policy moves those objects to an infrequent-access class at roughly half the price, automatically, with no application change.
tradeoffs: Retrieval carries a per-GB fee, so data read often costs MORE on this class
Minimum storage duration (30 days IA / 90 days archive) — deleting early is billed as though the object had stayed
First-byte latency rises on archive classes, from milliseconds to minutes
Objects under 128 KB are not worth transitioning; the per-object overhead outweighs the per-GB saving

advisory.name: Serve static assets from egress-free storage
advisory.summary: Hyperscalers charge for every gigabyte leaving their network. Cloudflare R2 and similar stores charge nothing for egress. Moving images, video and downloads there removes what is often the second-largest line on the bill.
tradeoffs: A second vendor to operate, monitor and pay
Cross-provider latency if the origin and the store are far apart
Not suitable for dynamic responses, only cacheable static objects
Data residency and compliance need checking separately
Migration effort for existing buckets and rewritten asset URLs

advisory.name: Cut egress before cutting compute
advisory.summary: Data leaving a cloud is billed per GB at a rate that does not fall with volume the way compute does. On media and analytics workloads it routinely exceeds the compute it serves, and it is the line least often forecast.
tradeoffs: Compression costs CPU on both ends, and for small responses the overhead exceeds the saving.
Co-locating a consumer to avoid egress may conflict with a data residency requirement, which is a constraint and not a preference.
Egress is the charge most likely to be a surprise, so reducing it also reduces the value of the alarm it would otherwise raise.

advisory.name: ARM-based managed cache nodes
advisory.summary: ElastiCache and its equivalents publish lower rates for Graviton node families than for the x86 ones at the same size, and a cache is a workload with no binary compatibility question at all.
tradeoffs: Node family availability varies by region; some smaller ARM sizes are not offered everywhere.
Changing node family is a replacement, so it needs a maintenance window or a warm secondary.

advisory.name: zram / zswap in-memory compression
advisory.summary: Compress memory pages in RAM instead of paging to disk, so the same workload fits on a smaller instance tier. Trades a little CPU for a lot of effective RAM.
tradeoffs: Costs CPU cycles; harmful if the workload is already CPU-bound
Benefit depends entirely on how compressible the workload's pages are
Not available on managed/serverless compute where you don't control the kernel
Must be load-tested before downsizing — do not downsize on theory

advisory.name: One NAT gateway unless a zone failure has to be survived
advisory.summary: A NAT gateway per availability zone is the right answer for a workload that stated it cannot go down. For one that did not, the second gateway is $41/month of standby nobody asked for.
tradeoffs: Losing the AZ holding the gateway takes outbound connectivity with it. Inbound traffic and anything already established survives, but patching, agent check-in and third-party API calls stop.
Cross-AZ traffic to reach the single gateway is billed, which claws back a little of the saving on chatty workloads.

advisory.name: VPC endpoints instead of NAT data processing
advisory.summary: Traffic from private subnets to S3, DynamoDB and the AWS APIs can take a private route instead of paying a NAT gateway to process every gigabyte.
tradeoffs: Interface endpoints bill per AZ per hour whether used or not, so a low-traffic workload can pay more for the endpoint than the NAT data it diverts. The engine's `_endpoint_plan` only adds them where the diverted volume justifies the hourly cost.
Each endpoint is another resource to manage and to get the security group right on.
Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB. Everything else needs the interface kind.

advisory.name: Cache reads instead of growing the database
advisory.summary: A cache node is materially cheaper per read served than the database instance it protects. Where the same rows are read repeatedly, caching them is cheaper than sizing the database for the traffic.
tradeoffs: Stale reads. Every cache is a decision about how wrong you are willing to be, and for how long.
Invalidation is application work, and getting it wrong is a correctness bug rather than a performance one.
Another component to run out of memory, fail over and monitor.

advisory.name: Cache reads so the database can be smaller
advisory.summary: Most read-heavy applications ask the database the same questions repeatedly. An in-memory cache in front absorbs those reads, which often means a database one or two sizes down carries the same traffic.
tradeoffs: The cache itself costs money and can erase the saving
Stale reads unless invalidation is done carefully
Cache stampede on expiry can hit the database harder than no cache at all
Adds a failure mode and an operational component
Application changes required; not a configuration switch

advisory.name: Serve repeat bytes from the edge, not the origin
advisory.summary: Origin egress is billed per GB at full rate. A CDN in front of it serves cache hits at a lower rate and stops the origin paying for the same object twice.
tradeoffs: Personalised or per-user responses cache poorly; a CDN in front of them is pure added cost.
Invalidations cost money and take minutes, so deploys need a cache-busting strategy rather than a purge habit.
Another hop to debug when something is stale.

advisory.name: Multi-AZ database only where downtime was said to matter
advisory.summary: Multi-AZ is a published SKU at roughly double the single-AZ rate, not a multiplier. It is required by a stated availability need and is pure cost without one.
tradeoffs: Losing the zone holding the single instance is an outage lasting as long as a restore. That is the whole trade, and it is only acceptable where the workload said so.
Single-AZ patching windows are user-visible; Multi-AZ ones are not.

advisory.name: A read replica only where reads actually dominate
advisory.summary: A replica doubles the database line. It earns that on a read-heavy workload and buys nothing on a write-heavy or low-traffic one, where it is a second instance kept warm to serve traffic that never arrives.
tradeoffs: A workload that later becomes read-heavy will need one, and adding it under load is worse than having it.
Replicas also serve as a failover target on some engines, so removing one can lengthen recovery even when it was not needed for capacity.

advisory.name: Size the fleet from the rate, not from a round number
advisory.summary: Instance counts chosen by habit -- three, or four, or "one per environment" -- are usually above what the stated rate needs. Sizing from the rate removes the difference.
tradeoffs: Sizing to the stated peak leaves no headroom for a peak that was understated, and traffic figures given from memory usually are.
An availability floor of two instances applies regardless, so this cannot take a highly available workload below that.

advisory.name: Right-size over-provisioned instances
advisory.summary: Most instances are picked once, generously, and never revisited. Matching the instance to observed utilisation is the least glamorous and most reliable saving available.
tradeoffs: Sizing to the average causes incidents at the peak
Needs real metrics; guessing smaller is not right-sizing
Requires a restart, so a maintenance window
Burstable instance families can mask sustained CPU need
The standby database roughly doubles the largest line on the bill
Still one region — a regional outage is not covered

tradeoffs: Personalised or per-user responses cache poorly; a CDN in front of them is pure added cost.
Invalidations cost money and take minutes, so deploys need a cache-busting strategy rather than a purge habit.
Another hop to debug when something is stale.

advisory.name: Multi-AZ database only where downtime was said to matter
advisory.summary: Multi-AZ is a published SKU at roughly double the single-AZ rate, not a multiplier. It is required by a stated availability need and is pure cost without one.
tradeoffs: Losing the zone holding the single instance is an outage lasting as long as a restore. That is the whole trade, and it is only acceptable where the workload said so.
Single-AZ patching windows are user-visible; Multi-AZ ones are not.

advisory.name: A read replica only where reads actually dominate
advisory.summary: A replica doubles the database line. It earns that on a read-heavy workload and buys nothing on a write-heavy or low-traffic one, where it is a second instance kept warm to serve traffic that never arrives.
tradeoffs: A workload that later becomes read-heavy will need one, and adding it under load is worse than having it.
Replicas also serve as a failover target on some engines, so removing one can lengthen recovery even when it was not needed for capacity.

advisory.name: Size the fleet from the rate, not from a round number
advisory.summary: Instance counts chosen by habit -- three, or four, or "one per environment" -- are usually above what the stated rate needs. Sizing from the rate removes the difference.
tradeoffs: Sizing to the stated peak leaves no headroom for a peak that was understated, and traffic figures given from memory usually are.
An availability floor of two instances applies regardless, so this cannot take a highly available workload below that.

advisory.name: Right-size over-provisioned instances
advisory.summary: Most instances are picked once, generously, and never revisited. Matching the instance to observed utilisation is the least glamorous and most reliable saving available.
tradeoffs: Sizing to the average causes incidents at the peak
Needs real metrics; guessing smaller is not right-sizing
Requires a restart, so a maintenance window
Burstable instance families can mask sustained CPU need
The standby database roughly doubles the largest line on the bill
Still one region — a regional outage is not covered
